## Why `glmap`?

<div class="glmap-eli5-box">
<span class="glmap-box-badge">🌱 ELI5 (Plain-English Mental Model)</span><br/>
<ul>
<li><b>One-Line Magic:</b> Give <code>glmap()</code> almost any spatial object in R (points, polygons, or a <code>terra</code> raster grid) and it figures out how to draw it automatically.</li>
<li><b>No More Color Functions:</b> In <code>leaflet</code>, you had to build a separate <code>pal &lt;- colorNumeric(...)</code> function and manually wire up a legend. In <code>glmap</code>, you just write <code>color = ~my_column, palette = "viridis"</code> and both the colors and legend appear automatically.</li>
<li><b>Instant Raster Sliders:</b> When you plot a <code>terra</code> raster, <code>glmap</code> sends the actual numbers to your graphics card. You can flip between palettes or turn on 3D hillshade shadows in the browser in <b>0 milliseconds</b> without waiting for R!</li>
</ul>
</div>

<div class="glmap-tech-box">
<span class="glmap-box-badge">⚙️ Technical Mode (C++17 + WebGL2 Pipeline)</span><br/>
Traditional R mapping packages built on <code>Leaflet.js</code> serialize spatial objects into GeoJSON text inside HTML and draw features using DOM/SVG/2D Canvas. When your dataset reaches <b>100,000 to 1,000,000+ features</b> or uses high-resolution <code>terra</code> rasters, R spends tens of seconds converting coordinates to text and the browser tab freezes.<br/><br/>
<code>glmap</code> eliminates the JSON and DOM bottlenecks entirely via C++17 <code>GLMP</code>/<code>GLMR</code> binary buffers, C++ <code>mapbox/earcut.h</code> polygon triangulation, and WebGL2 instanced SDF &amp; <code>RGBA32F</code> floating-point raster fragment shaders.
</div>

---

## 1. Instant One-Line Exploration

`glmap()` inspects your input (`sf`, `sfc`, `terra::SpatRaster`, `terra::SpatVector`, `wk::xy`, `nanoarrow`, `data.frame`, or `crosstalk::SharedData`) and automatically chooses the right GPU layer:

```{r}
library(glmap)

# Generate synthetic benchmark data
bench <- gl_benchmark_data(n_points = 100000L, n_polygons = 2000L)

# Instant GPU map of 100,000 points
glmap(bench$points_df, color = ~intensity, palette = "turbo", radius = 3)

# Instant GPU map of a Float32 DEM raster with real-time hillshading
glmap(bench$raster_mat, palette = "terrain", hillshade = TRUE)
```

---

## 2. Building Multi-Layer GPU Maps with Pipes (`|>`)

Use `glmap()` with `add_raster()`, `add_polygons()`, `add_lines()`, `add_points()`, `add_hexbin()`, `add_heatmap()`, and `add_labels()`:

```{r}
glmap(basemap = "dark") |>
  add_raster(
    bench$raster_mat,
    palette = "terrain",
    hillshade = TRUE,
    opacity = 0.65,
    group = "Terrain DEM (Float32)"
  ) |>
  add_polygons(
    bench$polygons_sf,
    fill_color = ~elevation,
    palette = "viridis",
    fill_opacity = 0.65,
    group = "Polygons (C++ Earcut)"
  ) |>
  add_hexbin(
    bench$points_df,
    hex_radius = 0.035,
    palette = "plasma",
    opacity = 0.75,
    group = "Hexbins (C++ 64-bit Hash)"
  ) |>
  add_points(
    bench$points_df,
    color = ~intensity,
    palette = "turbo",
    radius = 3.0,
    opacity = 0.85,
    group = "Points (WebGL2 SDF)"
  ) |>
  use_plugin("export_png")
```

---

## 3. Handling 1M–10M+ Features with In-Memory C++ Spatial Indexing or DuckDB

For massive datasets in interactive R or Shiny sessions, enable `dynamic_viewport = TRUE`, `transport = "server"`, or `add_duckdb()`. `glmap` builds an in-memory C++ spatial index (`gl_spatial_index()`) or queries DuckDB to stream only the features inside the current viewport with automatic Level-of-Detail (LOD) stride sampling:

```{r}
big_df <- data.frame(
  lon = runif(1e6, -75, -71),
  lat = runif(1e6, 45, 48),
  val = rnorm(1e6)
)

glmap(basemap = "dark", transport = "server") |>
  add_points(
    big_df,
    color = ~val,
    palette = "viridis",
    radius = 2.5,
    dynamic_viewport = TRUE
  )
```
